newsitem.title: USA: Quick turnaround for Motorola unlikely - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Quick turnaround for Motorola unlikely - analysts.

text.p: The stock of Motorola Inc. fell Tuesday after the technology giant dampened any hopes of a quick turnaround in its key industries.
"The turnaround which people were expecting is probably going to be late to happen," said Rakesh Sood, an analyst who follows communications technology companies for Hambrecht & Quist.

Citing continued weakness in a semiconductor industry swamped with overcapacity and stiff competition in other sectors such as cellular phones and modems, Motorola said it would take charges of "tens of millions of dollars" in the fourth quarter of 1996 as part of its effort to cut costs.
Motorola has also said it is reducing its work force, cutting back work schedules and halting building projects, among other things. The company withheld details on work force reductions.

"We need to finalise these actions, make the notifications that are required of those affected and then public statements would be made," Ed Gams, Motorola's director of investor relations, said in a conference call with analysts.
On Monday, the Schaumburg, Ill.-based company reported its third quarter earnings fell to $206 million, or 34 cents a share, from $496 million, or 81 cents a share, a year ago.

Revenues were $6.5 billion, down from $6.9 billion. This was the second consecutive quarter for which Motorola had reported lower sales, after having posted consistent growth since 1985, the company said.
"Pricing remains very competitive in all our major businesses, and we expect this to continue," Gams said.
Analysts cut fourth quarter and 1997 earnings estimates, and PaineWebber, for example, downgraded the stock to attractive from a buy rating.
Motorola fell $1 to $48.75 in composite New York Stock Exchange trading.

Gams said Motorola believed the semiconductor industry's recent recession may have bottomed out, but the company still expects year-over-year industry revenues to be lower for a few more quarters. Motorola said its semiconductor group essentially broke even in the third quarter.

He said Motorola expected industry-wide semiconductor revenues to grow by less than 10 percent in 1997 -- down from a previous estimate of 12 percent to 13 percent. Motorola pegged revenues for the worldwide industry at $145.9 billion in 1995.
"I was surprised by how poorly their semiconductor business did this quarter," said Lawrence Borgman, an analyst with Josephthal Lyon & Ross.
Nonetheless, most analysts said they were willing to stick with Motorola as a long-term investment.

"Our conclusion is that Motorola isn't any less of a great company -- it's just a technology company," said Doug Christopher, an analyst with Crowell Weedon. "They're a well-run company, their products are first rate, but a technology company will experience this kind of volatility. You have to be patient in the near term."
